sections.text: This is our whole bill for ten days. Seventeen dollars, seventy-eight cents. The number that matters is not on it.
Every tool you approve is priced by the month or by the seat. Your work does not happen by the month. It happens in runs.
So divide the bill by the number of times the task actually ran. Ours ran eight hundred and eighty-nine times. Two cents a run.
Here is the line that repeats every week. Last week, a hundred and thirty accounts, one page each. Two dollars sixty. That is the number to defend, not the plan name.
What the bill leaves out: our own machine time, and sixteen cents we paid twice because a run broke halfway and eight answers had left the cache.
Two cents a run is nothing. Two cents a run, six hundred times a day, is another conversation. Price the run, then decide.
Before the next renewal, count how many times that task ran last month, then divide. Send this to whoever signs.

strategy.audience: Non-technical small-business leader, AI level 0-6 of 10 (POSITIONING.md §4): an owner, operations lead or team lead in a 5-50 person company responsible for one repeated process. Specifically the person who approves and renews software spend.
strategy.concept: We open our own ten-day bill on screen - seventeen dollars and seventy-eight cents, eight hundred and eighty-nine paid units at two cents each - and do the one piece of arithmetic a pricing page never does: divide the bill by the number of times the task actually ran. Then we volunteer what the bill leaves out, including the sixteen cents we paid twice when a run broke halfway.

filter.ai_boundary: The machine performs the run and prints what it will cost before it starts. The human sets the cap, reads the ledger and decides when the price stops being worth the task; no tool is allowed to spend without an explicit confirmation.
filter.friction: Pricing pages quote per seat or per month and the work happens in runs, so the person who signs has no unit to compare against. The bill grows with use and the growth stays invisible until the invoice lands.
filter.next_action: Take one repeated task, count how many times it actually ran last month, divide the bill by that number, and only then renew.
filter.process: Approving or renewing a paid tool that runs one repeated task in the business - the weekly report, the batch of quotes, the inbox triage - where the invoice arrives monthly and nobody in the company can say whether it is expensive.

strategy.objective: Get one viewer to count how many times their repeated task actually ran last month and divide the bill by it before the next renewal, so they walk into that conversation with one number instead of a plan name.
strategy.promise: One number you can defend to whoever signs, worked out on our own bill in front of you.
strategy.rationale: cost_money is the largest pain cell in the analysed corpus (n=48, 33 creators) and money-not-spent framing sits above the corpus median on save rate (0.0306 against 0.0250, p=0.007), while money-earned framing costs reach (view_lift 1.19 against 2.12, I-25) - this reel is on the profitable side of that line. Nobody in the 266 analysed reels shows their own bill: 84 carry a money-saving desire (01-general-conclusions §B) and 71 frame the outcome as money (I-25), and in both cells the money is somebody else's price rather than the author's own ledger.

title: Cost per run, not price per month

traceability.evidence_summary: Everything on screen is our own ledger: ten entries between 1 and 10 September 2026, 889 paid units at $0.02, $17.78 total, of which the repeating weekly line is 130 accounts at one page each for $2.60, and sixteen cents were paid twice after a run broke partway through. cost_money is the largest pain cell in the analysed corpus (n=48, 33 creators) and money-not-spent framing sits above the corpus median on save rate (0.0306 against 0.0250, p=0.007) while money-earned framing costs reach (view_lift 1.19 against 2.12, I-25). The four references contribute structure only: DaGTeJNN1GR (9.3x lift, 30.2 shares/1k) the measured amount in the opening sentence shown on a real screen, DcUNlNvy6J9 (22.2x, 42.9 saves/1k) the three-part metered-pricing pain with the caption chip pinned to the exact cell, DbVq4mwz38L (32.8x, 54.0 saves/1k) the volunteered caveat straight after the cost claim, Dc_TX1CttIc (24.1x, 31.7 shares/1k, ungated) the announce-then-earn-the-verdict ordering with an economic close. Opening on the screen rather than the face is worth roughly half again the forwarding rate (I-09: 0.0213 against 0.0140, creator-normalised +0.285, p=0.00025).
traceability.original_synthesis: Nobody in the 266 analysed reels shows their own bill; 84 carry a money-saving desire (§B) and 71 frame the outcome as money (I-25), always somebody else's price rather than their own ledger. The itemised ledger, the single division, the repeating weekly line item and the volunteered duplicate charge are ours and reproducible line by line from reports/data/spend.json.
traceability.why_better_than_generic: A generic AI script would compare three tools' pricing pages and warn about hidden costs. This one performs a single division in front of the viewer on a real bill, isolates the repeating line item that a renewal conversation actually turns on, volunteers the sixteen cents we wasted, and refuses the savings claim the format invites - which POSITIONING.md §6 forbids and which the reach data (I-25) says costs distribution anyway.
